It begins with rain. Not theatrical, but a slow gray seep that makes the windowpane look like old glass breathed on by a ghost. I sit at a desk I have never fully trusted, because it wobbles when I think too hard, and I am trying to find the first word of this thousand-word assignment. First word is hardest, because it pretends to be a beginning. But there are no beginnings, only the middle of things, and I have walked into it with wet shoes.

Outside, a woman in a yellow coat walks a dog that refuses to hurry. The dog stops at every puddle, not to drink, but to consider its reflection. I understand that dog. It wants to know if the wet world has changed its face. I want to know that too. Every time I sit down to write, I am checking whether the rain has changed my face, whether small days have made me unrecognizable to myself.

The rain taps the glass like a nervous visitor. I think about the letters I have not written, the calls not made, the apologies rehearsed but never delivered. There is cruelty in silence. It is not an absence; it is a presence that grows heavier with each day. The things we do not say become furniture. We arrange our lives around them.

The dog has moved on. The woman checks her phone. Maybe she is reading a message from someone who loves her, or maybe she is checking the weather. Both are forms of hope. Hope is the most stubborn human invention. It survives on almost nothing—a sliver of sky, a warm cup, a memory of laughter. It persists like a weed through concrete.

I once knew a man who collected umbrellas but never used them. He said an umbrella was a promise to the sky: I will not let you touch me. But he liked to be touched. He walked in rain with his face tilted up, waiting for benediction. I think of him now because I am trying to decide whether to open the window. The desk would warp, but I would feel something other than the radiator’s hum.

Writing is a way of letting the rain in without opening the window. It is a controlled flood. You sit in a dry room and invite the weather of your mind to make a mess. Then you spend hours cleaning it up, arranging the puddles into sentences, wringing out the excess. Sometimes you drown anyway. Sometimes you float.

The rain has softened. The woman and the dog have disappeared. I imagine them going home to a small apartment where the dog shakes itself off and the woman hangs her yellow coat. She will make tea. She will sit by a window and wonder if she has made the right choices. But she will not know that I have imagined her, that she has become a character in a stranger’s thousand words.

That is the strange power of attention. To be seen, even from a distance, is to be changed. I do not know her name or if she is happy. But for a few minutes she was the center of my world, and I gave her a dog, a yellow coat, a quiet dignity. We do this all the time. We turn strangers into stories, invent motives, project our loneliness onto their faces. The man on the bus becomes a widower; the woman at the café an artist who lost her muse.

But here is the truth: I am tired of imagining other people. I want someone to look out a rainy window and see me walking with no umbrella, and wonder where I am going, and give me a story I do not have to write myself. Is that too much to ask? Probably. The world does not owe us a narrative. We build our own, sentence by sentence, out of whatever the rain leaves behind.

The radiator clicks. The room smells of old paper and wet wool. I think about the thousand words I have been given. They are almost spent. I have used them to describe rain and a dog and a woman in a yellow coat and a man who collected umbrellas. I have not solved anything, but I have paid attention. Maybe attention is the only real prayer.

There is a word I like: solitude. It comes from the Latin for “alone,” but it does not mean loneliness. It means being alone in a way that is full, not empty—the difference between a vacant house and a room where someone is thinking. I am in that room. You are in it with me, even if you read this years from now, even if the rain has stopped, the dog has died, the yellow coat has faded. Because writing is time travel. It lets me sit beside you and say: I was here. I was thinking. I was trying to make sense of the rain.

Now the sky is lighter. The rain has stopped. The window is still closed, but the world outside looks newly washed, as if forgiven. I could go outside, feel the wet grass, find the woman in the yellow coat and tell her she was in a story once. But I won’t. The story is better if she never knows. Some things are meant to be seen from a distance, through glass, while the kettle cools and afternoon folds into evening.

I have reached the end of the words I was given. There is always more to say—another memory, another confession. But a thousand words is a small room. I have filled it with furniture, arranged the chairs, hung the coats, and left the door slightly open, because I am not ready to say goodbye. The last word is a lie. It pretends to be an ending. But there are no endings, only the middle of things, and I have walked out of it with wet shoes.
